summary: Joel Becker introduces METR as an independent nonprofit researching AI capabilities and catastrophic risks. He frames the talk around reconciling two conflicting sources of evidence: benchmark-style evidence and economic-style field evidence. The first METR paper measures AI ability to complete long tasks using 'time horizons.' Instead of traditional benchmarks like SWE-bench or GPQA—which suffer from saturation and interpretation problems—METR gathers human baseline data on diverse tasks spanning software engineering (HCAST), atomic problems (SWAR suite), and novel ML research challenges (REBench). Humans are experienced but low-context. The 'time horizon' is the human completion time at which the model succeeds 50% of the time. Plotting time horizons against calendar time reveals a remarkably steady exponential trend, doubling approximately every six to seven months, holding through models like GPT-5.1 CEX max. However, Becker notes three benchmark limitations: humans are low-context, benchmarks have low ceilings and saturate quickly, and tasks are not messy enough. To address these, METR designed a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 16 experienced developers—on average the third top contributor to repositories averaging a million lines of code with 10+ year histories—each completing about 16 real GitHub issues randomly assigned to AI-disallowed or AI-allowed conditions. Developers were provided Cursor Pro with Claude 3.6/3.7 Sonnet. Economics experts predicted ~40% time savings, developers predicted ~24% beforehand and ~20% afterward, but the actual result was a 19% slowdown when AI was allowed. METR investigated hypotheses through screen recordings. Contributing factors include overoptimism about AI usefulness, implicit repository context and high developer familiarity (experts already know solutions and are limited by typing speed), lower AI performance on large complex repositories, and low AI reliability requiring verification and correction. Caveats include the unusual developer population, concentration in March 2025, and small study size. Becker discusses multiple explanations for the benchmark-field gap: reliability needs to be 95-99% to save time, benchmark-style scoring differs from holistic mergeability scoring, high-context experts make AI relatively less advantageous, task distributions differ in messiness, suboptimal capability elicitation in Cursor versus METR's optimized agents, and interdependence across tasks requiring humans to maintain context across subtasks. METR is continuing this work and hiring research engineers, scientists, and a director of operations.

sections.title: Introduction to METR & The Capability Gap
sections.summary: Joel Becker introduces himself as a researcher at METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research), an independent nonprofit assessing AI catastrophic risks. He frames the talk around reconciling two conflicting evidence sources: benchmark-style evidence from METR's time horizon paper and economic-style evidence from a developer productivity RCT.

sections.title: The Problem with Current Benchmarks (Saturation & Interpretation)
sections.summary: Becker explains difficulties with traditional benchmarks like GPQA: interpreting what percentage scores mean in terms of real capability is hard, and benchmarks saturate quickly, leaving less time between useful signal and full saturation.

sections.title: METR's New Methodology: Human Time Horizons
sections.summary: METR gathers human baseline data on diverse tasks from HCAST (software tasks requiring autonomy), SWAR suite (atomic problems), and REBench (novel ML research challenges). Humans are experienced but low-context. AI performance is measured on the same tasks, and capability curves are fit to predict the human completion time at which models succeed 50% of the time—the 'time horizon.'

sections.title: Empirical Results: Fitting Capability Curves
sections.summary: Claude 3.7 Sonnet achieves near-100% success on tasks under 4 minutes and declines on harder tasks. The 50% success point defines the time horizon. This pattern is robust across models and task distributions.

sections.title: Time Horizon Trends: Claude 3 Opus vs. o1-preview
sections.summary: Plotting time horizons against calendar time reveals a remarkably steady exponential trend. Claude 3 Opus has a ~4-minute horizon, o1-preview ~15 minutes. The trend has held through GPT-5.1 CEX max, with time horizons doubling every six to seven months.

sections.title: Benchmark Limitations & Motivation for Field Evidence
sections.summary: Becker identifies three benchmark limitations: low human context, low ceilings with rapid saturation, and lack of messiness in tasks. To address these, METR designed an RCT with 16 experienced developers on mature open-source projects, each completing ~16 real GitHub issues randomly assigned to AI-disallowed or AI-allowed conditions.

sections.title: Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) Discussion
sections.summary: Developers were provided Cursor Pro with Claude 3.6/3.7 Sonnet. Repositories averaged 1M+ lines of code with 10+ year histories; developers were on average the third top contributor with ~5 years personal history. Economics experts predicted ~40% time savings, developers predicted ~24% beforehand and ~20% afterward, but the actual result was a 19% slowdown when AI was allowed. METR reviewed many hours of screen recordings to investigate.

sections.title: Reconciling the Gap: Why High Benchmarks Don't Mean High Productivity
sections.summary: Becker presents contributing factors: overoptimism about AI usefulness, implicit repository context and high developer familiarity making typing the bottleneck, lower AI performance on large complex repositories, and low AI reliability requiring verification and correction. He notes caveats: the study population is unusually expert, the experiment is concentrated in March 2025, and it is a small study. Alternative explanations include developers lacking AI tool familiarity, hourly pay reducing urgency, and statistical noise.

sections.title: Explaining the Discrepancy: Context, Reliability, and Task Interdependence
sections.summary: Becker proposes several explanations for the benchmark-field gap: reliability needs to be 95-99% to save time; benchmark-style scoring differs from holistic mergeability scoring; high-context experts make AI relatively less advantageous; task distributions are messier in reality; suboptimal capability elicitation in Cursor versus METR's optimized agents; and task interdependence requires humans to maintain context across subtasks.

sections.title: Future Work & Hiring at METR
sections.summary: METR is continuing this line of work with longer tasks, more ambitious RCTs, and additional evidence sources. They are hiring research engineers, research scientists (including scrappy startup people), and a director of operations at metr.org/careers.
